entries.sentence: The NHS lists stress, urge, mixed and overflow incontinence, and a GP can talk through treatments such as pelvic floor exercises and bladder training.
entries.note: Types listed; pelvic floor muscle training and bladder training are conservative treatments; GP advised for any type.

entries.sentence: The NHS describes stress incontinence as leaking under pressure, such as when coughing or laughing, and urge incontinence as leaking after a sudden, strong need to pee.
entries.note: Stress: leaks under pressure e.g. coughing, laughing; urge: leak after sudden intense need to pee.

entries.sentence: The NHS advises seeing a GP about any type of urinary incontinence.
entries.note: NHS advises seeing a GP for any type of urinary incontinence.

entries.sentence: Treatments tried first include lifestyle changes, pelvic floor muscle training and bladder training, with medicines and surgery for some people.
entries.note: Conservative options first: lifestyle changes, pelvic floor training, bladder training; medication and surgery options exist depending on type.

entries.sentence: NICE guidance for women says clinicians classify the type of incontinence at the first assessment and use bladder diaries.
entries.note: NG123: at first assessment classify as stress, mixed or urgency/overactive bladder; use bladder diaries.

entries.sentence: Sudden loss of bladder control with back pain, numbness or leg weakness is an emergency, and NHS Scotland advises calling 999 or going to A&E.
entries.note: NHS Scotland: call 999 or go to A&E for loss of bladder or bowel control, saddle numbness, or weakness in both legs (cauda equina syndrome).

entries.sentence: The NHS lists several types of urinary incontinence, and they have different patterns.
entries.note: NHS lists stress, urge, mixed, overflow and total incontinence.

entries.sentence: In stress incontinence, leaks happen when the bladder is under pressure, for example when coughing or laughing.
entries.note: Stress incontinence: leaks under pressure such as coughing or laughing.

entries.sentence: In urge incontinence, a sudden, intense need to pee comes first, and urine leaks before the toilet is reached.
entries.note: Urge: leaks following a sudden intense need to pee.

entries.sentence: Mixed incontinence is a combination of the two.
entries.note: Mixed incontinence listed as less common type combining stress and urge.

entries.sentence: Overflow incontinence, which the NHS also calls chronic urinary retention, happens when the bladder cannot empty fully.
entries.note: Overflow incontinence (chronic urinary retention): bladder cannot fully empty.

entries.sentence: The NHS also lists total incontinence, which is sometimes described as severe, continuous leaking.
entries.note: Total incontinence listed; described as severe and continuous leaking.

entries.sentence: The NHS says stress incontinence is usually linked to weak or damaged pelvic floor muscles, or damage to the muscle that keeps the urethra closed.
entries.note: Stress incontinence: weak or damaged pelvic floor muscles and urethral sphincter.

entries.sentence: Urge incontinence can come from a problem with the detrusor muscles in the bladder wall, and one NHS trust lists bladder irritation from infection or medicines, nervous system conditions and anxiety.
entries.note: North Tees and Hartlepool NHS trust page: detrusor muscle problem; irritation from infection or medication; nervous system diseases; anxiety.

entries.sentence: The NHS lists pregnancy and vaginal birth, being overweight, family history, constipation and getting older among the factors that raise the chance of leaks.
entries.note: Risk factors listed: pregnancy and vaginal childbirth, obesity, family history, constipation, increasing age.

entries.sentence: Some medicines can also affect bladder control, and the NHS says a GP may advise whether changing them could help.
entries.note: Some medicines (ACE inhibitors, diuretics, some antidepressants) can affect bladder control; stopping if a doctor advises may help.

entries.sentence: The NHS says urinary incontinence can usually be diagnosed after a talk with a GP.
entries.note: Diagnosis usually follows a consultation with a GP.

entries.sentence: The GP asks about symptoms and may do a pelvic or rectal examination.
entries.note: GP asks about symptoms; may carry out pelvic or rectal examination.

entries.sentence: A GP may also suggest keeping a bladder diary, which records how much is drunk and how often urine is passed.
entries.note: NHS: GP may ask for diary of fluid intake and urination frequency; NICE: bladder diaries used at initial assessment.

entries.sentence: The GP may also check for causes such as a urinary tract infection.
entries.note: GP may rule out causes such as a urinary tract infection.

entries.sentence: The NHS advises seeing a GP for any type of incontinence, so that the type and likely causes can be worked out.
entries.note: NHS advises seeing a GP for any type; purpose of finding type from the consultation.

entries.sentence: The NHS and NHS inform describe simpler approaches as the usual starting point.
entries.note: Conservative options usually tried first.

entries.sentence: These include treating an underlying cause, lifestyle changes, pelvic floor muscle training and bladder training.
entries.note: Conservative options: treating cause, lifestyle changes e.g. less caffeine, pelvic floor training, bladder training.

entries.sentence: Lifestyle changes can include cutting down on caffeine, and one NHS trust suggests water or decaffeinated drinks in its place.
entries.note: Reducing caffeine listed as lifestyle change; trust suggests water, squash or decaffeinated drinks.

entries.sentence: The same trust lists artificial sweeteners, fizzy drinks and alcohol as other possible bladder irritants.
entries.note: Trust lists artificial sweeteners, fizzy drinks, alcohol as possible bladder irritants.

entries.sentence: One NHS trust says that straining to poo can weaken the pelvic floor muscles.
entries.note: Trust page: straining to poo weakens pelvic floor muscles; attributed to trust page not NHS England.

entries.sentence: For urge symptoms, a GP may prescribe a medicine called an antimuscarinic if bladder training has not helped.
entries.note: Antimuscarinic may be prescribed for urge if bladder training not effective.

entries.sentence: For stress incontinence, a medicine called duloxetine is one option that has been described, and the sources say it should not be stopped suddenly.
entries.note: Duloxetine is one option for stress incontinence and must not be stopped suddenly.

entries.sentence: Pads are not a treatment, but they may be useful while waiting for an assessment or for a treatment to start working.
entries.note: Summary: incontinence pads are not a treatment but might help while waiting; attributed to NHS trust leaflet, page not certain.

entries.sentence: Surgery depends on the type, and the options listed include sling procedures and bulking agents injected near the urethra for stress incontinence.
entries.note: Surgery for stress: sling procedures and urethral bulking agents; bulking agent injected into walls of urethra.

entries.sentence: Pelvic floor muscle training is a programme of exercises for the muscles that support the bladder.
entries.note: Pelvic floor muscle training programme; doctor may refer to specialist, usually physiotherapist.

entries.sentence: The NHS says a GP may refer someone to a specialist, usually a physiotherapist, to start a programme.
entries.note: Doctor may refer to a specialist, usually a physiotherapist, to start a programme.

entries.sentence: Bladder training aims to lengthen the gap between feeling the urge to pee and actually going.
entries.note: Bladder training aims to lengthen the gap between the urge and going.

entries.sentence: A pelvic floor programme and bladder training are described as first-line approaches, and they work best when kept up consistently, according to one NHS trust.
entries.note: Search summary: pelvic floor exercises and bladder training frequently first-line, can improve symptoms when consistent; trust source. Attribution uncertain between pages.

entries.sentence: NICE has guidance called urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse in women, which covers the management of both.
entries.note: NG123 title: Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse in women: management.

entries.sentence: At the first assessment, NICE says clinicians classify the incontinence as stress, mixed, or urgency or overactive bladder.
entries.note: NG123: classify as stress, mixed or urgency/overactive bladder at first assessment.

entries.sentence: NICE advises bladder diaries in this first assessment.
entries.note: NG123: use bladder diaries in the initial assessment.

entries.sentence: For urgency or mixed incontinence, NICE names bladder training lasting at least six weeks as the first treatment.
entries.note: NG123: bladder training for a minimum of 6 weeks is first-line for urgency or mixed incontinence.

entries.sentence: NICE also says duloxetine is not a first treatment for women whose main problem is stress incontinence.
entries.note: NG123: duloxetine is not a first-line treatment for women with predominant stress urinary incontinence.

entries.sentence: NICE does not recommend absorbent pads or similar products as a treatment for incontinence.
entries.note: NG123: absorbent containment products, hand-held urinals and toileting aids not offered to treat incontinence.

entries.sentence: It also says devices placed inside the vagina or urethra are not used for routine management.
entries.note: NG123: intravaginal and intraurethral devices not used for routine management.

entries.sentence: Sudden loss of bladder control together with back pain, numbness or weakness in the legs can be a sign of cauda equina syndrome, which NHS Scotland treats as an emergency.
entries.note: NHS Scotland: loss of bladder or bowel control, saddle numbness, weakness in both legs; cauda equina syndrome emergency guidance.

entries.sentence: NHS Scotland advises calling 999 or going to A&E straight away.
entries.note: NHS Scotland advises calling 999 or going to A&E immediately.

entries.sentence: Blood in the urine is a different matter.
entries.note: Separate NHS symptom page.

entries.sentence: The NHS says it is not usually serious but can sometimes be, so it needs checking, and it advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or getting help from NHS 111.
entries.note: NHS: not usually anything serious but sometimes can be; get it checked by GP; urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.

entries.sentence: Common causes include urinary tract infections, kidney stones and an enlarged prostate.
entries.note: Common causes include UTIs, kidney stones and an enlarged prostate.

entries.sentence: For leaks without these signs, a routine GP appointment is the route the NHS describes.
entries.note: NHS advises seeing a GP for any type of urinary incontinence.
